THE SYSTEM OF THE FINITE VERB IN CLASSICAL BIBLICAL HEBREW Peter J. Gentry University of Toronto
This article provides a comprehensive description of the verbal system of classical biblical Hebrew, explaining how tense, aspect, and modality are signaled and correlating form and function in a way that accounts adequately and simply for the entire range of usage. A sensitive balance is maintained between synchronic and diachronic analysis. Also considered are communicative constraints, such as discourse grammar, pragmatics, and contextual meanings versus implicature. The base forms are primarily aspectual, with temporal deixis a function of aspectual default and discourse setting. Integrated within the model is a fresh proposal for understanding so-called volitives in classical biblical Hebrew. Normally command forms in Hebrew are considered a unified system of volitives consisting of cohortative, imperative, and jussive. Following up on the work of Niccacci, Revell and more recently Shulman on (so-called) modal forms in Hebrew, it is argued that the volitives should not be viewed as a unified system. Rather, projective modality apart from imperative forms is signaled by position of the verb. This in itself is not new. It is further argued, however, that the -āh suffix normally considered to be the marker of the cohortative functions in a manner similar to the Akkadian ventive and has nothing to do with projective modality. The explanatory power of this proposal is such that it can explain the distribution of the -āh suffix on all verb forms in the Hebrew Bible as well as forms usually eliminated from discussion as extrasystemic or corruptions in the text. Striking support, moreover, is found in the Amarna Canaanite texts.
INTRODUCTION
All who read the texts of classical biblical Hebrew—students and scholars alike—continue to be perplexed and troubled by the nature of the Hebrew verbal system. Indeed, Leslie McFall aptly summed things up in the title of his 1982 work: The Enigma of the Hebrew Verbal System.

usage—whether common or marginal. Beginning students are confused; they have entered a strange world. Only one thing seems to be certain: the system is definitely non-Indo-European. Scholars with extensive experience in reading the texts may provide accurate explanations of difficult passages, but once again, combining practice with theory in a consistent manner is elusive. Even in the most recent standard textbook, An Introduction to Biblical Hebrew Syntax by B. K. Waltke and M. O'Connor, where discus- sions of the uses of the verb are contextually determined, correlation be- tween the described semantics of the verb and the different categories of usage is not always apparent or straightforward.
Recent developments, however, do give hope of overcoming the prob- lem. New approaches and disciplines as well as refinements of the philolog- ical tradition, whether applied in combination or separately, continue to advance our understanding of the verbal system of classical biblical Hebrew. The discipline of linguistics offers new approaches, categories, and models. Cross-linguistic studies provide a framework for describing how human languages work. Categories such as tense, aspect, and modality have been clarified and refined as well as the way in which different human languages code these parameters. Discourse grammar has focused on fea- tures of the language operating beyond the level of the individual sentence on the discourse as a whole. Pragmatics has delineated ways in which lan- guages encode in their structure the relationship between context and lan- guage. A consensus concerning the Hebrew verb is beginning to emerge from applying such tools to classical biblical Hebrew. In addition, similar tools are being applied to cognate languages and as the corpus of inscrip- tional texts increases, so does the power of comparative linguistic study.
This paper attempts to describe the Hebrew verbal system by (1) giving a linguistic orientation for understanding the verb, (2) interacting with past theories and building on recent studies, (3) correlating form and function in a model which accounts adequately and simply for the range of usage.
At the heart of an adequate description of the Hebrew verb is an ade- quate correlation of form and function. Several constraints affect such a description.

(1) How does the verbal system signal categories of tense, aspect, and mood or modality? Indeed, does the Hebrew system signal all of them or only a selection? The categories and the linguistic strategies for marking them must be identified.
(2) Both diachronic and synchronic analysis must be carried out and a balance of the proper contribution of each to the description as a whole maintained. Gropp, for example, notes that most twentieth century scholars have a diachronic solution in mind and complains that the synchronic question is inadequately addressed.D. M. Gropp, “Function of the Finite Verb,” p. 45. True enough! Yet an approach which does give proper priority to synchronic analysis must at the same time incorporate the firm results of diachronic study and also be guided by appropriate cross-linguistic parameters in proposing what strategies are employed to signal categories of tense, aspect, and modality. Gropp’s own hypothesis that the forms signal relative tense is one where analysis is focused synchronically—although that is, perhaps, a counsel of despair. From a diachronic perspective he points out that while previous proposals frequently assumed just two basic forms—prefix and suffix—recent studies are beginning to distinguish various prefixed paradigms. So, like the description given below, he distinguishes a couple of prefixed paradigms as well as perfect from converted perfect. By contrast, this description, while maintaining the priority of synchronic study, (a) incorporates in a better and fuller way the diachronic evidence Gropp briefly references, (b) is more probable from a cross-linguistic perspective, and (c) includes data he explains away as either extrasystemic or corruptions in the text.
(3) The communicative constraints of discourse grammar and pragmatics must be accounted for properly. Among many important studies in the last twenty years, those of Buth and Dempster, Niccacci and Revell have contributed significantly to the model proposed below. One such communicative constraint is the type of discourse, for example, conversation or historical narrative.For the distinction, see A. Niccacci, The Syntax of the Verb in Classical Hebrew Prose, trans. W. G. E. Watson (Sheffield: JSOT Press, 1990) and especially his further refinements in A. Niccacci, “On the Hebrew Verbal System,” in Biblical Hebrew and Discourse Linguistics, ed. R. D. Bergen (Dallas: Summer Institute of Linguistics, 1994). A language may maintain an economy of forms by employing one form for different functions in mutually exclusive discourse types. The use of the so-called short prefix for jussive in direct speech or preterite in historical narrative may be an example of economy of this

sort.9 Another constraint is sequencing.10 Hebrew employs two devices operating in tandem: (a) the absence or presence of waw and (b) the order of constituents in a sentence. The last mentioned linguistic strategy is also linked to another constraint: theme or topicality. Initial position in a sentence may be loosely described as topical. In narrative, it is almost always occupied by the verb, because the sequence of events constitutes the theme. When initial position is occupied by a clause component other than the verb, a change in topic is signaled, but also a discontinuity in the event-line or narrative. Gropp notes the importance of distinguishing general meanings of verb forms from contextual meanings or implicatures.11 Due account of discourse grammar and pragmatics will provide clear criteria for such distinctions.12
FORM AND FUNCTION IN A LINGUISTIC MODEL OF THE HEBREW VERBAL SYSTEM
No space can be given here for a detailed history of previous theories. It is sufficient to note that for a long time the system of the verb was understood to signal primarily two categories of tense: past (suffix) and non-past (prefix).13 This understanding was abandoned for about a century and a half in favor of an aspectual theory also based on two categories: perfective (suffix) and non-perfective (prefix).14 Both approaches have proponents in recent studies, although a high proportion of them represent a return to a system based primarily on tense.15
To be sure, historical narrative may include direct speech and vice versa. Sequencing refers both to the continuity of events in a narrative and to the formal relation of propositions in direct speech (see S. G. Dempster, “Linguistic Features of Hebrew Narrative: A Discourse Analysis of Narrative from the Classical Period,” [Ph.D. dissertation, University of Toronto, 1985] 32–34). D. M. Gropp, “Function of the Finite Verb,” p. 46. See especially B. Comrie, Tense (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1985), pp. 18–26. Gropp lists the forms and their meanings and distinguishes contextual from general meanings (see D. M. Gropp, “Function of the Finite Verb,” pp. 57–58). Nonetheless, a model of the verb where the forms signal anteriority or relative tense does not easily explain the contextual meanings or what signals them. See R. Buth, “The Hebrew Verb in Current Discussions,” Journal of Translation and Textlinguistics 5 (1992) 92–93 and L. McFall, Enigma, p. 17. These categories, however, and the theories which produced the terms perfect and imperfect differ—as DeCaen shows—from the definition of these terms today (for which, see below). See V. Historically, we have essentially three paradigms, short prefix (yaqtul),19 long prefix (yaqtulu), and suffix (qatala). Sequential and Non-Sequential are categories of discourse grammar and pragmatics described and refined helpfully by Buth.Sketched briefly already in R. Buth, “Hebrew Poetic Tenses and the Magnificat,” JSNT 21 (1984) 67–83 and detailed independently (with some variations) in S. Dempster, “Linguistic Features of Hebrew Narrative.” Initial position is topical. In contrast to focus, a device for marking important information in a clause, topic marks the narrator’s intended perspective for contextualizing the clause, that is relating it to the discourse. The Sequential forms, wayyiqtol and wəqatal, are employed to encode continuity or to foreground information in the discourse. By definition, the forms require initial position for the verb; hence the foreground of a narrative is the chain of events. Non-Sequential signals a break in the event-line indicated by both a clause constituent preposed to the verb and a different pair of verbs marking aspect and tense, that is, [x] qatal and [x] yiqtol.The symbol [x] stands for a clause component such as Subject, Object, or Modifier occupying the initial position. Thus Non-Sequential functions pragmatically to signal background, a category which Buth describes succinctly:

TENSE AND ASPECT
The categories of tense and aspect as applied to the Hebrew verbal system by Buth and others may be refined somewhat. Tense and aspect represent different points of departure in the human description and representation of time in language.
Tense may be defined as the presentation of time as points in a sequence; hence the focus is on notions of precedence and subsequence. Gropp’s description is to the point: “‘Tense,’ as generally understood, is a deictic category.”See D. M. Gropp, “Function of the Finite Verb,” p. 53 n. 20, B. Comrie, Tense, pp. 33–18 and Binnick’s critique, (R. Binnick, Time and the Verb: A Guide to Tense and Aspect [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991], pp. 126–132). That is, it is an element within the text that points to the speech situation. If the point of reference is the moment of speaking, we have a system of absolute tense; if the point of reference is not identical to the moment of speech, we have a system of relative tense.
Aspect, as Hendel states, is concerned with the differing perceptions of an event, either seen from without as a bounded whole (perfective) or from within as an unbounded process (imperfective).R. S. Hendel, “Margins of the Hebrew Verbal System,” p. 164; cf. R. Binnick, Time and the Verb, pp. 207–214, 458. Aspect, then, may be defined as the relationship between an event and the frame within which it is

perceived or viewed. If the event is seen as a whole within the frame of the viewer, then it is perceived globally; conversely if the boundaries of the event (either beginning or end) extend outside of the frame of the viewer, then the event is perceived as an ongoing process.
The fundamental opposition between both pairs (that is wayyiqtol-wəqatal and [x] qatal–[x] yiqtol is one of aspect: perfective versus imperfective respectively. The tense or temporal deixis is secondary, being determined by a combination of aspect and the discourse framework. If the discourse framework is narrative, then the tense is past.

This interpretation of Judg 3:23 (see also 2 Sam 13:18) is bound to be questioned by some. Longacre argues that wəqatal may mark climactic or pivotal status here rather than a ‘frequentative’ meaning.29 His apparently alternative interpretation does not disprove the present hypothesis, but rather supports it. The approach here can be defended as follows. First, from a synchronic point of view, [x] yiqtol and wəqatal are in complementary distribution and so must consistently function the same way, in historical narrative just as in direct speech. It is standard theory to distinguish a conjunctive wə + qatal from wəqatal, with the former functioning as [x] qatal and the latter as [x] yiqtol, but contextually or syntactically no clear or simple set of signals have been identified to prove such a distinction for classical biblical Hebrew.30 Unless we adopt an approach which bleaches the form of any semantic value,31 we ought to assume the form has the same basic meaning everywhere. Second, to assert that the form in historical narrative is imperfective and past does not mean that the meaning is always frequentative or progressive. Imperfective aspect may either (a) subsume several types of imperfective aspect32 or (b) signal a different discourse function as, for example, in Greek.33 Strong cross-linguistic evidence abounds as well as evidence from within classical biblical Hebrew that the tense-aspect of a verb may code not only lexical-semantic and propositional-semantic features, but also discourse-pragmatic features.34 If the discourse framework is conversation, the perfective normally defaults for past tense while the imperfective defaults for non-past tense.

MODALITY
Some discussions of the verbal system in Hebrew classify usage as either indicative or modal.So E. J. Revell, “The System of the Verb.” This terminology is somewhat misleading, since it suggests that the indicative is a non-modal category. The present study considers language as a flexible tool in the mouth of the speaker, by which he or she describes his or her experience of reality or attempts to manipulate reality. Thus, the indicative is not to be crudely equated with the real world or with events in the real world; rather it indicates what the speaker asserts to be real or an event in the real world. Broadly speaking, modality may be divided into three categories: (1) assertive, (2) epistemic modality, and (3) deontic modality.See T. Givón, Syntax, p. 318. Hendel’s definitions are useful:
Deontic modality (from Greek deon, “that which is binding”) involves the speaker’s will, as in statements of wish, command, permission, or obligation. These kinds of utterances express the speaker’s desire or decision concerning an action. Epistemic modality (from epistēmē, “knowledge”) involves that speaker’s opinion or knowledge about a proposition, as in statements of doubt, belief, or other shades of expectation or opinion. Epistemic utterances relate to the speaker’s state of knowledge, rather than to the speaker’s will.R. S. Hendel, “Margins of the Hebrew Verbal System,” p. 169.
Two basic categories are defined for the system of the finite verb in classical biblical Hebrew in the model being proposed: (1) Assertive,The term ‘assertive’ indicates a modality where one asserts or claims an event to be real. Whether, in fact, the event is real is not at issue. It is asserted to be real by the speaker. and (2) Projective.T. Givón, Syntax, p. 318 employs the term ‘manipulative’ instead of ‘projective.’ This modality involves projecting one’s desires, intentions, wishes, or will in some way onto the map of reality. Assertive forms are employed for both assertive and epistemic modality, the latter use being frequently distinguished from assertion by additional particles, rather than distinct forms. The projective category covers deontic modality.

Since Joüon51 and Bergsträsser,52 followed by Lambdin53 and Waltke and O’Connor,54 forms commonly called cohortative, imperative and jussive have been considered a single and unified set of projectives labeled volitives. Imperatives are second person volitives, cohortatives are first person volitives, and jussives are third person volitives (also second person, since the imperative cannot be employed with negation, that is in prohibitions [with לא] and vetitives [with אל]). The model which is presented here differs significantly from this standard view.
Recent research by Niccacci, independent studies by Revell for Judges-Kings, and a doctoral dissertation by Revell’s student Ahouva Shulman all indicate that apart from imperatives, which are distinguished by form, Hebrew marks projective modality for first and third person verbs, that is cohortatives and jussives, by position. Revell lists approximately 40 instances in Judges-Kings where prefix forms in initial position, not marked as cohortative (הָ- suffix) or jussive (yiqtol-S), are semantically projective.55 Shulman claims that only 61 out of 1515 imperatives, 6 out of 102 3rd person jussives, and 5 out of 197 cohortatives are non-initial.56
Consideration of the prehistory of the verb, as researched by scholars such as Moran and Rainey and evaluated by Huehnergard, reveals that there were separate prefixed forms: yaqtul was perfective and yaqtulu was imperfective. As Huehnergard suggested, projective modality was marked at the level of the phrase; the linguistic strategy employed for this was word order. Thus, for prefix forms, initial position in conversation is projective; non-initial position is assertive.

Description of the Function of Projectives in Hebrew
Second Person Projectives
The only projective verbs in classical biblical Hebrew formally marked as such are forms which are exclusively second person and inflected for gender and number. Commonly called imperative, this form is aspectually perfective and normally in initial position. If a second person projective with imperfective aspect is required, a long prefix in initial position is used to mark it. This, indeed, is rare. For a sequence or series of second person projectives, wə + imperative is used for perfective aspect, while wəqatal is employed for imperfective.
The imperative verb form is not used with negatives. Instead, vetitives are indicated by אל plus short prefix (for perfective aspect) while prohibitions (for imperfective aspect) are signaled by לא plus long prefix. Since distinguishing short and long prefix forms is impossible in most roots (that is, the forms are neutral), it is the negative (אל or לא) which clearly identifies the form as either short or long prefix.

Third person projectives are also marked by initial position, not by a specific form or a modal morpheme attached to the stem of the verb. Where short and long prefix forms can be distinguished, the short prefix forms mark perfective aspect while the long prefix forms mark imperfective aspect. However, modal imperfects are clearly and consistently distinguished from indicatives (n. 9 above). I would argue that this formal/syntactic distinction must be held to reflect a distinction in function, even if that function is not consistent with “universal’’ semantic categories. Cf. S. R. Driver A Treatise on the Use of the Tenses in Hebrew (3rd edn, Oxford, 1892), p. 212. The standard use of the contrasting forms was, however, continued, so that the short and long forms acted as allomorphs, the use of which was conditioned by the position of the verb in the clause. This is seen in Dan. xi, where imperfects appear in short form at the beginning of a clause whether jussive or indicative value is expected. Within a clause, long forms are used. The only excep- tion is the qere form in Dan. xi 10. First person modals, the affixed imperfect forms, also characteristically begin their clauses. All examples in Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, can be understood as having modal value, but it is clear that, in the late biblical period, the formal contrast between affixed and ordinary imperfect forms no longer distinguished modal from indicative value, and the same is true at Qumran (Qimron, p. 44). It is reasonable to suppose,
FIRST PERSON IMPERFECT FORMS WITH WAW CONSECUTIVE 423
then, that these affixed forms came to be perceived as positional variants of the ordinary imperfect, equivalent to the short forms in 2nd and 3rd person. Consequently the affixed forms were also used with waw consecutive.11
The use of affixed 1st person forms with waw consecutive represents, then, a syntactic or semantic development which was standardized in a post-exilic form of literary Hebrew. It is possible that some parts of the Bible were written in a Hebrew of this sort in which the standardization of this usage was either less complete than at Qumran, or has been obscured by later change. In the book of Nehemiah, however, the use of these forms distinguishes sections different from those of the usual literary division based on content and style. If the latter division is justified, the use of affixed 1st person forms with waw consecutive shown in the MT must have arisen during the process of transmission. This conclusion must apply to the use of these forms throughout the Bible. They cannot be taken, in any book, as certainly representing the language of the author.
The long form of the 1st person imperfect from roots IIIh is regularly used where a cohortative form is expected. The use of long 1st person forms from these roots with waw consecutive is more common in later materials, and shows a distribution generally similar to that of affixed 1st person forms from other roots with waw consecutive. Such long forms are not used with waw consecutive in any of the five possible cases in Neh. ii 10-20 and iv. They are used in one of two cases in Neh. i 1-ii 9, and in all four cases in the rest of the book. They occur in 1/2 cases in Judges, in all five in 2 Samuel, in 2/3 cases in Ps. lxix (there are no cases in the other Psalms listed above) and in 1/2 cases in the poetry of Job. Consequently the use of the long form of the 1st person imperfect with waw consecutive in roots IIIh can reasonably be regarded as representing the same development as does the use of the affixed form in other roots. The use of long 1st person forms is, however, much more common generally than is that of affixed forms. Long

It seems clear that the stress patterns of these forms reflect a natural phonological development in which stress position was conditioned by syllable structure. The exception in Neh. iv 3 forms a negligible proportion even of 1st person forms. The vowel patterns suggest a correspondingly regular development. The vowel of a final closed syllable in these forms originally acted as short. In hollow root forms, and in hifʿil forms from other roots, the vowel of this syllable changed in quality in all forms but those in which both penultimate and antepenultimate syllable were open (with the few exceptions noted). Where the vowel of this final closed syllable was stressed u or i, it was, in later times, often marked with a vowel letter, but there is no way of knowing to what extent the use of these letters in any part of the MT represents that of the work in its original form.
The use, in category (3), of long first person singular forms with waw consecutive is thus due to a phonological development quite distinct from the syntactic/semantic development which led to the use of affixed first person forms, both singular and plural, in categories (1), (3), and (4), and most probably also the use of long first person forms, also both singular and plural, in category (2). Both developments appear to have occurred towards the end of the biblical period, but there is no adequate basis for dating them either absolutely or relative to each other. The lack of relationship between the two developments is made clear (apart from the fact that both occur in category (3)) by the occurrence of two exceptional long 1st person forms with waw consecutive in Neh. iv 3 and iv 9, in a passage characterized by the failure to use affixed forms. Less striking confirmation is provided by the regular use of vowel letters in the final closed syllable of forms from category (3) in 1 Samuel (x 18, xii 1, xxviii 21) where an affixed form occurs in only one of twelve possible cases (or 4/15 if long IIIh forms are included).
This survey has, then, the negative merit of stressing the dangers of using 1st person forms with waw consecutive as criteria of authorship. The use of affixed forms cannot be attributed with any confidence to any biblical author. The use of long 1 s. forms from hollow roots (and others in category (3)) was characteristic of later biblical Hebrew generally. This represents a development separate from that which gave rise to the use of affixed forms, not a different

The System of the Verb
in Standard Biblical Prose
E.J. Revell

This article surveys the system of the verb in the Former Prophets starting from the premises (advanced by others) that there are two indicative “tenses”, each represented by a “simple” and a “consecutive” form in complementary distribution, and one modal system, represented by the imperative, jussive and cohortative forms, also in complementary distribution. The main thesis is that the indicative and modal systems are fully independent because (1) imperfect forms with modal value are distinguished from indicatives by their position in the clause, (2) a perfect form with waw “consecutive” following a modal has a value different from that of a modal in the same position. The article begins with a survey of the indicative system intended to set this thesis in its proper context by showing that (1) the value of any verb form depends heavily on its syntactic/semantic context, (2) despite the distinct values of the “tenses”, in many contexts either may be used to represent the same occurrence — the choice is determined by the viewpoint of the author, or by the particular implications he intends to convey. The article concludes with a survey of the way this system developed to the end of the Biblical period.

THE USE OF INDICATIVES
2.1 The meaning carried by the opposition of the two categories of the indicative, QTL and YQTL, has been much debated. It seems to me that it is most easily presented as one of time reference: QTL ‘past’ versus YQTL ‘present/future’. While the ease of such presentation is no doubt partly due to the fact that English uses a tense system, there is no real reason to suppose that Hebrew does not.
(a) The fact that forms typically representing past time may represent future, and vice versa, under particular conditions, does not show that the basic system is not one of tense (pace Driver, 1892, #1). The same phenomenon occurs in English, as in the examples in Lyons (1986), p. 239.
(b) The criterion by which the value of a form must be judged is not its historical origin, but its use within the corpus. No matter what the origin of the waw consecutive verb forms, those which occur in the corpus must be regarded as syntactically conditioned variants of the perfect and imperfect forms. This removes any obstacle to considering the categories they represent as tense categories, as argued in Blau, 1970.
(c) The Hebrew of post-biblical times certainly used a tense system, and the same is widely assumed for the ancestor of the biblical language, as vestigially represented by the ‘preterite’ (or waw consecutive) use of the imperfect form. It seems likely, a priori, that the system of the intervening period would also have been one of tense. The QTL:YQTL

Judg. 1:20 ויתנו לכלב את חברון כאשר דבר משה ‘They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses (had) said.’

3.4 As the translations show, English can use verbal phrases which accurately reflect these different temporal relationships. Where the context is future, however, a simple present form ‘unless I tell you,’ ‘the land to which they are carried’ would be more usual, and a simple past form ‘I did’ would be adequate in most cases where the context is present or past. The difference between the usages possible in English is basically social. The use of more or less precise forms would carry information about the educational background of the speaker, or the social context of the speech. Similar differences are possible in Hebrew. An action which is past in relation to a future event may be represented by a QTL form, as in the examples noted above. It may also be represented by a YQTL form, as
Judg. 6:26 והעלית עולה בעצי האשרה אשר תכרת ‘You will send up an offering with the wood of the Asherah which you will (have) cut down.’ It is at least reasonable to suggest that the verb form is chosen to reflect one of the possible views of the temporal relationship of the event. A YQTL form shows that it is perceived in relation to the speaker, and so as future; a QTL form shows that it is perceived in relation to its context, and so as past. The choice of forms could no doubt be similarly justified if the QTL:YQTL contrast were explained in terms of ‘complete:incomplete,’ or ‘punctual:durative’ action. What is significant for this paper is the fact that the choice of verb forms does not depend wholly on the time or nature of the action. Where the action can be understood as belonging to either of the contrasting categories, either form can be used, according to the impression of the time or of the nature of the action that the speaker wishes to convey.

In hypothetical situations in quoted speech, a QTL form is occasion-ally used to represent an action which has not (yet) occurred, apparently to indicate that the action in question is unlikely or undesirable (see Driver, 1892, #19.2. although he does not connect this with his discus-sion of the conditionals in #138.i), as in 2 Sam. 15:33 אם עברת אתי והית עלי למשא ‘If you were to go over with me, you would be a burden to me.’ This contrasts with the use of YQTL forms standard in future conditions, as in the following sentence, where the preferred action is indicated 2 Sam. 15:34 . . . ואם העיר תשוב . . . והפרתה לי ‘But if you return to the city . . . you can frustrate the counsel of Ahitophel for me.’ Similarly, in 2 Kgs. 7:4, the perfect forms in ואם אמרנו . . . ואם ישבנו (‘if we were to say . . . if we were to remain . . .’) clearly present courses of action undesirable to the speaker. Judah uses it in his emotive appeal to his father in Gen. 43:9 . . . אם לא הביאתיו ‘If I don’t bring (perfect) him (Benjamin) back . . . ,’ but not in the quite different spirit in which he describes the scene to Joseph in Gen. 44:32 . . . אם לא אביאנו ‘If I don’t bring (imperfect) him . . . ’ Here again the choice of a QTL or a YQTL form depends on the way the speaker perceives, or wishes to present, the situation.

THE USE OF INDICATIVE FORMS: YQTL
8. In terms of tense, YQTL forms refer to the present or future. Thus, in quoted speech, in a present context,
Judg. 1:1–2 מי יעלה . . . יהודה יעלה ‘Who will go up? . . . Judah will go up.’ Where the context is past, a YQTL form may represent an event which is present or future relative to the past context, as
Judg. 17:8 וילך האיש . . . לגור באשר ימצא ‘The man went to live where he could find a place.’ The English translation represents the different time reference of the two verbs by the use of the modal ‘could’ for the

If the first action were future, the second Hebrew verb would not change in form, because the relationship of the two actions to each other would still be the same. However, the English translation must change to ‘He will go to live where he will/can find a place’ to indicate the different temporal relationship of the second action to the speaker.

Other examples occur in Judg. 6:4, 10:4, 11:40, 12:5, 14:10, etc. Where the context is past, QTL forms can be used instead of YQTL to represent these habitual actions (see #4, and cf. e.g. Judg. 2:18–19 with Judg. 3:6). THE IDENTIFICATION OF MODAL FORMS
13. The modal system is represented by imperatives, used in affirmative clauses with second person subject, and by the forms of the imperfect known as "jussive" and "cohortative" used where the clause is negative, or where the subject is first or third person. Distinct modal imperfect forms occur only where the subject is first person, 2m.s., or 3m./f.s. Any original difference between the modal and the indicative forms of the imperfect has been lost where the subject is 2f.s., 2.pl, or 3.pl. (On forms with suffixes, see #14.3.) First person modal forms show the affix הָ—; the corresponding imperfect forms do not. Forms from roots IIIh show the "long" imperfect form (identical with the indicative imperfect form) where a first person modal is expected. In 2m.s. and 3m./f.s. forms, where the imperfect form shows î or û in a final closed syllable, the corresponding modal form shows e or o respectively. Where the final syllable of the imperfect form is open, modal imperfect forms from roots IIIh omit the final vowel. The same form from roots IIIʼ is used in all situations. These forms from roots IIIʼ, first person forms from roots IIIh, and all other forms which show no modal/indicative distinction, are referred to here as "neutral" forms. First person modal imperfect forms are called "affixed". Second and third person forms are called "short" in contrast to the "long" indicative forms. A form is said to have "modal value" if used in a position in which the standard system permits the use of modal forms but not indicative forms, as after the negative אַל.
(11) Some have been explained as examples of standard usage, but the explanations do not seem plausible. E.g., Driver (1892, #37β) regards the imperfect ימצאכה in 1 Kgs. 18:10 as corresponding to English ‘He could not find you,’ contrasting it with the perfect which would represent ‘He had not found you.” Johnson (1979:55), who suggests that the imperfect stresses the attempt without implication for its result, presumably has much the same idea as Driver. However, the activity represented by the verb, whatever it may have been, is the subject of an oath, and must have occurred before the time of swearing. If the oath was, in fact ‘I have not been able to find ...,’ one would expect the use of the verb יכל.

It is therefore reasonable to restate Orlinsky’s conclusion as, “Where two clauses stand in sequence, and the first has a modal verb form, if the second clause begins with a verb, it may be a modal form, a neutral imperfect with modal value, or a perfect with waw consecutive.”
14.5 The combined force of these considerations seems fully to justify the assertion made above. An imperfect which begins a clause has modal value; an imperfect which stands within a clause (and is not preceded by אל or followed by נא) has indicative value.

MODAL VERBS AND THE waw consecutive perfect
17. The material in #15-16, which lists the cases in which the use of imperfect forms marked as modal or indicative appears to be inconsistent with the conclusion reached in #14, provides no serious reason to doubt that conclusion. Consequently it can be stated that an imperfect form in the corpus, which begins its clause has modal value; an imperfect form which stands within its clause (and is not preceded by אל or followed by נא) has indicative value. Clearly, then, the waw consecutive perfect could only be a free variant of the modal imperfect, since it also begins its clause. It could, however, be a conditioned variant of the indicative imperfect; that is, it could have the grammatical function of representing a YQTL indicative verb in clause-initial position. That this would be a useful function is obvious. The main factor conditioning word order in biblical Hebrew is ‘thematization’. The components of a clause are arranged in the order of their significance for the speaker or narrator.For the term ‘thematization,’ see Leech, 1981, p. 195. The importance of this factor is suggested by the traditional statement that an item was placed before the verb “for emphasis.” It is demonstrated in detail for constituents following the verb in Lode, 1984, and for verbless clauses in the corpus, with examples from verbal clauses, in Revell, 1989. Modal verbs, which present commands, requests, etc. are typically the most significant component of their clause, and so stand first in it. However the significance of other verbs also often requires that they stand first in their clauses, particularly where sequences of events are depicted. Hence the need to distinguish modal from indicative verbs. The fact that the waw consecutive perfect is used to distinguish a clause-initial verb as a YQTL indicative is suggested by the following considerations.
17.1 In conditional sentences in which the apodosis begins with a waw consecutive perfect verb, the only function of the particle waw is to mark

the perfect form as ‘consecutive’. An apodosis which does not begin with a waw consecutive perfect is typically not introduced by a conjunction.21
17.2 A waw consecutive perfect form follows an imperative in only about a quarter of the possible cases in the corpus, and follows a modal imperfect in little more than a tenth.22 In sharp contrast, clause initial verbs which carry on a sequence of indicatives are regularly waw consecutive in form. A waw consecutive perfect following a modal verb cannot, then, stand in the same sort of relationship to it as it does to a preceding indicative. Consequently it is reasonable to argue that the waw consecutive perfect represents the YQTL indicative as a conditioned variant of the imperfect, as suggested in #1. If this view is correct, a waw consecutive perfect following a modal verb must have connotations different from those of a modal verb in the same position. A survey of the use of the waw consecutive perfect suggests that this is indeed the case.

19.5 The waw consecutive perfect is translated as an imperative in accordance with English usage in this case, as in the others, but the use of this form shows that the verb is a YQTL indicative, with connotations different from those carried by an imperative or other modal form. A modal form is used to present a forceful command, whether its force reflects the fact that, although not first in a series of commands, it is of major significance, or reflects the urgency of the situation, or the social or moral status of the speaker relative to the person addressed. The waw consecutive perfect (a YQTL indicative form) is used in the same context to present a command which is less forceful, whether the (relative) lack of force reflects the fact that the action to be taken is a later consequence of action already forcefully commanded, or that it is not urgent, or that there is no wish to mark any difference of social or moral status between the speaker and the person addressed. It must be admitted (with Joüon, 1947, 301) that the different values of the waw consecutive perfect and imperative following an imperative are not always significant in the contexts in which they are used. Similarly, in English, the four possible variations of ‘I sang/was singing as I walked/was walking’ could be used in the same context with no significant difference of connotation. That does not mean, however, that the two past forms have the same meaning. So also the simple equation “after an imperative, waw consecutive perfect = imperative” is an oversimplification; it hides the function of the waw consecutive perfect as presenting a clause-initial indicative, with its particular connotations. Just as with QTL and YQTL forms, which are typically used in different contexts as having distinct values, and which present different connotations in those contexts in which either can be used, so with the two forms with present/future value: modal and YQTL indicative. In a context established as one in which directions are given by a preceding imperative (or otherwise as 2 Sam. 14:10, 1 Kgs. 13:31, quoted in #20.2), either an indicative or an imperative form can be used, and the connotations they present are different.
20.1 Where the verb does not begin the clause, the YQTL category must be represented by an imperfect form. This is used after an imperative with the same connotations as a clause-initial waw consecutive perfect; that is, it presents a continuation of the command in a less forceful register. As is well known, לא with the imperfect is used in early materials to present a particularly forceful prohibition.This usage does not seem to be current in the corpus. לא and אל appear equivalent in 1 Kgs. 20:8 אל תשמע ולוא תאבה ‘Do not listen and do not agree.’ Similarly in 2 Sam. 5:23 לא תעלה ‘do not go up (to attack)’ is not a particularly forceful command. A modal verb is not used in the same context in יהודה יעלה ‘Judah will go up’ (Judg. 1:2). The negatives אל and לא appear to vary freely in prohibitions at Qumran. (See Qimron, 1986:400.13*) However it is obvious that, both in early materials and in the corpus, לא with an imperfect can present a statement, as well as a command. In
2 Sam. 21:17 ...לא תצא... ולא תכבה ‘Do not go out to battle with us any more, and you will not quench the lamp of Israel’.
The translation of one verb as a command and the other as a statement is a matter of English usage, reflecting an understanding of the content of the clauses and their context. There is nothing in the form of the verbs or their syntax which requires translation in either way. Similar usage is found in Akkadian, where lā taparras can present either a command or a prediction. The same is true of ‘you will not do’ in English. In the latter case, the two values are distinguished by intonation patterns, as well as by the context in which they are used. In written texts, only the latter criterion is available. As for the relative forcefulness of the indicative and imperative patterns, this depends on the conventions of the users. My own impression is that in English, as in Hebrew, the statement ‘You will not do’ typically presents a more forceful prohibition than the imperative ‘do not’, whereas the imperative ‘do’ presents a more urgent command than the statement ‘you will do’.

HISTORICAL CONSIDERATIONS
23. The above survey shows that a plausible case can be made in support of the contention that waw consecutive perfect forms represent clause-initial YQTL verbs, and that indicative verbs carry a meaning distinct from that of modals. That this case is valid, and not merely plausible, can be argued from the changes which occurred in the verb system of later Biblical Hebrew, as shown in the books of Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The use of verbs in these books can be briefly described as follows.
23.1 The use of QTL forms does not differ significantly from that of standard prose, but there is a morphological innovation. First person imperfect forms with waw consecutive commonly show affixed ָה-. This is a late usage which became standard in the Hebrew of Qumran (see Qimron, 1986, #310.122, and Revell, 1988).
30 E. J. REVELL [30]
23.2 Imperfect forms in clause-initial position are regularly short, affixed, or neutral; those used within clauses are regularly long or neutral. However this formal contrast does not mark any semantic difference, as is shown by the fact that second person imperfect forms may begin clauses (Dan. 9:25, 12:13, also Neh. 9:28 in a past context).This use of verb forms is characteristic of Daniel 11, as in Dan. 11:17, 18, 25. Short imperfect forms are also used at the beginning of a clause with (apparent) indicative meaning in Dan. 8:12, 9:25. In Ezra-Nehemiah there are no passages dealing with the future where this usage could be shown. The same phenomenon is usual at Qumran. See Qimron, 1986, #310.129. It is also noteworthy that although the “H form” and “N form” suffixes are both used on imperfect forms at Qumran, the basis of their use is different from that described in #14.2. (See Qimron, 1986, #322.143). There are some exceptions. Affixed first person forms fail to occur where expected in Neh. 2:18, 5:12, 6:10, 10:32 (cf. #15.1). A long 3rd person imperfect form begins a clause which is closely related to the preceding in Dan. 12:12 אשרי המחכה ויגיע ‘Blessed be he who waits and reaches...’; also Dan. 12:4; and, in a past context, Neh. 3:14. Presumably the close semantic relationship (possibly reflected in intonational contours) shows that the verb is indicative (see #15.3, 4). The same usage may account for the long qere form in Dan. 11:10 ישב ויתגרה ‘He will return and wage war’. A long clause-initial imperfect occurs where no such relationship obtains in Dan. 12:13 (2m.s.) and Neh. 3:15 (qere, 3m.s., with past value). A short imperfect form occurs within a clause in Dan. 9:16 (before נא), Ezra 1:3 (after an extraposed constituent), and in Neh. 3:37, 13:14, after the negative אל where it begins the clause. However a long form is used after אל in Neh. 3:37 where it does not begin the clause.
23.3 The use of imperative forms follows the standard pattern, including that of the sequence of modals (#14.4). One imperative follows another in 22 cases. An imperative follows a jussive (marked by following נא) in Neh. 1:11. A jussive (marked by אל) follows an imperative in Neh. 3:37, as does a neutral imperfect in Dan. 1:12. The perfect with waw consecutive is not used in sequence with imperatives.
23.4 (Apart from use after imperatives) the waw consecutive perfect and the imperfect with conjunctive waw are free variants in clause initial position, as can be seen from the mixture of forms in sequence in Dan. 11:5, 7, 10, 15, etc.This also occurs in materials from Qumran, as in 1QS 4:20-21 ... ואז יברר ... וזקק ... ויז; but the waw consecutive perfect seems usually to be used to represent a clause initial future indicative at Qumran, as in the standard usage of the corpus.
24.1 In the form of language represented by Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, then, modal forms are still generally restricted to initial position

in the clause, and indicative forms to medial position, but it is clear that the contrast in form and position no longer marks any semantic distinction. It could be argued that the anomalies listed in #16.3, 4, show that the language of the corpus was already close to this situation, and that the different connotations ascribed to modal and indicative forms in many other cases are illusory. Thus שוב עמי ואשתחוה (with an imperfect in modal position 1 Sam. 15:25) and שוב עמי והשתחויתי (with a YQTL indicative, 1 Sam. 15:30) could carry exactly the same message ‘Return with me and I will worship’ (although they could show a shift from modal to indicative to express greater politeness/humility; see #20, especially Judg. 6:17 in #20:2). However the fact that different grammatical categories may, in some cases, be used without distinction does not show that they are never distinct. The difference of implication exists potentially in all cases, even though it may not be significant in all.
It has been shown above that the semantic fields of the two indicative categories overlap in a number of cases, so that either can be used to represent an action where such overlap occurs. The categories are, however, distinct in meaning; each carries connotations different from the other. Consequently, the possibility of choosing either category in such a situation allows the narrator to extend his range of expression beyond the limitations of morphology, and present a range of temporal or aspectual nuances comparable to that achieved in Indo-European languages through the greater variety of forms. The use of YQTL forms in sequence with modals, or in other situations in which they appear to present commands, etc. is an example of the same phenomenon. The fact that modal and indicative forms are occasionally used in the corpus without appreciable difference in meaning may reflect the beginning of the development which led to the complete loss of distinction between them, but not more than the beginning. The indicative and modal categories in the corpus are no less distinct in meaning than are the QTL and YQTL categories.
24.2 The distinction of the modal or indicative value of neutral imperfect forms by their position in the clause must have been a firmly fixed feature of the language, since it still governs the position in which short and affixed imperfect forms, or long imperfect forms, are used in Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, even though the forms do not differ in meaning. The use of verbs in these three books also differs from that standard in the corpus in some other respects. The waw consecutive perfect is not used after imperatives. Elsewhere, it is a free variant of clause-initial imperfects, and so has no special function. Second person

imperfects are used in clause-initial position, and an indicative imperfect form may be used where an imperfect is medial in a semantic unit, even where it is initial in a clause. These features suggest a considerable de- velopment from the pattern standard in the corpus towards the usage characteristic of Mishnaic Hebrew. It seems clear that a major cause of this development was the loss of distinction between the modal and in- dicative values of the imperfect.
THE SYSTEM OF THE VERB IN STANDARD BIBLICAL PROSE
25. A verb can be marked as modal in the corpus by its form (imper- ative, or short or affixed imperfect), by its position (initial in its clause) or by co-occurrence (with following נא or preceding אל). Any one of these marks will serve to identify it, but it may have two, or even three of them. A YQTL indicative is marked by a waw consecutive perfect form in clause-initial position, or by an imperfect form (not in co-occurrence with נא or אל) within a clause.
25.1 It is possible that the different modal forms in Hebrew are ves- tiges of more complete “imperative”, and “short”, and “affixed” imper- fect paradigms, each of which had a distinct function. In standard He- brew prose, however, they form a single set of modal forms, and in many cases the same “neutral” imperfect form is used for both modal and indicative functions. Due to the relation between the significance of a constituent and its position in the clause (see #17), verbs with modal value typically stood in clause-initial position. Consequently indicative imperfect forms came to be restricted to position within the clause, so that the value of a neutral imperfect was marked as modal if it began the clause, as indicative if it did not (unless it was marked as modal by a particle). The waw consecutive perfect (the origin of which is not known) came to be used where a YQTL indicative verb was required in clause-initial position, and so as a positional variant of the indicative imperfect. While this pattern continued to govern the positions in which the modal and indicative forms of the imperfect were used, the differ- ence in their values was lost, so that the imperative eventually became the only distinct modal form, as in Mishanic Hebrew. This development may be foreshadowed in the partial blurring of the distinction between the values of modal and indicative forms in the corpus. It was possibly influenced, in its later stages, by the vernacular language. The devel- opment resulted in the abandonment of the features which had distin- guished modal imperfects from YQTL indicatives, including the use of the waw consecutive perfect, because it took away their function. This

[33] process is quite advanced in the language of Qumran (see Qimron, 1986, #400.03*; Kutscher, 1974:357–8).
26. A QTL indicative is represented in the corpus by a perfect form within a clause, or at the beginning of a clause where the conjunction waw is not used. Where the conjunction is used, the QTL indicative is typically represented by the waw consecutive imperfect. This form derives from the original “preterite”, which early became restricted, in prose, to initial position in a clause which was part of a sequence, or was presented as such, and so began with a conjunction. Here it acts as a positional variant of the perfect, and functions to indicate the structure of narrative passages. The perfect form with a prefixed conjunction represents QTL in a past context in a number of cases in which the action is considered as identical with, or as a facet of, that of the preceding clause. This is distinct from the waw consecutive use of the perfect (which is restricted to a present/future context) and is common enough in the corpus that it can be regarded as a feature of standard usage. It is possible that, in an earlier phase, the waw consecutive imperfect was the only representative of QTL used in clause-initial position with a prefixed conjunction, and that this use of the perfect was the first symptom of the change which eventually led to the complete replacement of the waw consecutive imperfect by the perfect. However this may be, the waw consecutive imperfect appears to have been used according to the standard pattern throughout the biblical period and also in the literary language of Qumran. In 1QIsaa its replacement by the perfect is rare in comparison to the number of cases in which the waw consecutive perfect is replaced by the imperfect (see Kutscher, 1974:354–5, 357–8).
27. The use of verbs in the corpus is, then, a complex, but generally consistent system representing a more or less stable stage of usage characteristic of the prose narrative of a particular period. Since it is a stage in continuing development, it is not surprising that the usage is not entirely consistent. Possibly some of the unusual features found in it are vestiges of the usage of earlier stages, restricted, like English subjunctives, to particular contexts. Others may well be early examples of usage which became standard in the succeeding stage. No doubt some of the anomalies it shows arose from errors in transmission. The standard pattern of the usage is, however, clear. The most interesting feature brought out by this survey is the grammatical function of the waw consecutive perfect, which marks a clause initial verb as a YQTL indicative.
